content: The portion size of food products consumed daily at a population level, along with their sodium content (e.g., salty condiments), can significantly impact public health. If available, data on product sales volumes can help identify commonly consumed products that would have the greatest population-wide benefit if their sodium levels were reformulated or reduced. To achieve this, countries should aim to collect sales volume data, if available, to identify products that are widely consumed and would have the greatest impact on sodium reduction efforts. The methodology for developing sodium benchmarks is detailed in the report, with additional information on the development of regional benchmarks provided in Supplementary File 1. Clarifications and additional details regarding the methodology have been included in the report. Sodium ranges for product categories, such as the 25th, median, and 75th percentiles, have been provided. The 25th percentile represents the sodium content below which 25% of products fall, while the 75th percentile represents the sodium content below which 75% of products fall. This approach is more appropriate than providing the lowest and highest sodium levels in a category, as extreme values may result from labeling errors or unique products. Providing sodium content plots from different South-East Asian countries in this report is not considered beneficial for countries adapting these targets. Instead, an example of how frequency plots were used is provided, such as sodium levels for the nuts, seeds, and kernels category, as detailed in the methodology. The use of interquartile ranges (25th to 75th percentiles) is preferred over full ranges to avoid the influence of outliers. Additionally, summary statistics for each food category, including the mean, median, 25th percentile, and 75th percentile, are provided in Supplementary File 1.
